docs.title: Strata
docs.text:
Strata is a design for a systems language that keeps Rust's memory safety and Goose's compiler-managed arenas, and asks the programmer for far less ceremony. It aims at servers: many cheap virtual threads, shared caches, deterministic cleanup, and no lifetime annotations.

Status

Exploratory. There is no compiler yet. The .stra files in the repository are Strata as it would be written, and the C beside them is what a compiler would emit, written by hand and kept honest by tests and benchmarks.

docs.title: What this site is
docs.text:
A record of how the design got where it is: what was measured, what was decided and why, and what turned out to be wrong. Each step started as a question and ended as a number or a rule.

Start the journey{ .md-button .md-button--primary } Decisions so far{ .md-button }

docs.title: The design in six lines
docs.text:
1. Ordinary values carry no reference-count header; new makes a strong Ref<T>, and WeakRef<T> breaks cycles.
  2. Lifetimes are inferred, not written.
  3. Shared state is accessed through sync (read) and mutate (write) blocks; entering one may park the virtual thread.
  4. Nothing is hidden except virtual threads and parking: no implicit buffering, batching or retry.
  5. Every unbounded input has a declared limit, enforced before the data is held.
  6. Errors are exceptions declared with throws; cleanup never parks and never throws.

The full text is strata-design.md.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Rules the design has settled on, with the reason each was chosen.

Decision Why Nothing hidden except virtual threads and parking Programs stay predictable; batching and buffering must be asked for. Every unbounded input has a declared limit Memory is bounded before data is held; big bodies are streamed or spooled. No biased reference counting in v1 Equal or worse once objects cross threads; confined types get plain counts. Per-type arenas, no compaction Segregates lifetimes; addresses stay stable, which the lock order relies on. Chunk epochs in resident chunk headers MADV_DONTNEED zero-fills decommitted generation words. MADV_NOHUGEPAGE on stack pools With transparent huge pages a 64 KB stack costs 65 KB resident. Errors are exceptions with throws Throwing is visible in signatures; no throws clause means nothing escapes. Cleanup never parks and never throws It runs on every exit path, including unwinding. sync/mutate acquisition parks, FIFO Fairness, and workers keep running other vthreads. Spin briefly before parking Pure parking lost up to 75% of throughput under mixed load. Multi-object heads acquire all-or-nothing Mis-ordered heads cannot deadlock. Default slow-subscriber policy: Disconnect Never silently loses messages; Notice is available. Not yet confirmed by the user. Strata identifiers are camelCase User preference. Constants stay UPPER_CASE; generated C may use underscores. Syntax: T?, methods in types, optional self, Pattern -> {} arms Avoids Rust-isms. No third-party crates in converted programs Strata would have no equivalents. Strata source and C live in separate folders stra/ is Strata only; c/ is runtime and compiler-output stand-ins.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Are all Ref<T> counts atomic by default, or can compiler-proven confinement use plain counts, and how is migration to shared ownership kept safe?
  • Is sync/mutate required for every Ref<T>, or only for those that may cross tasks, and how is shareability declared?
  • When does a growable array get a dedicated virtual region instead of a relocatable buffer?
  • Exact string representation, slicing and UTF-8 indexing.
  • How does a throw interact with a scope that still has child vthreads?
  • Stack model: fixed reserve with guard pages, or segmented stacks.
  • How are exported lifetime and effect metadata versioned?

docs.title: Not yet built or measured
docs.text:
• Any compiler. Everything here is hand-written C beside .stra source.
  • The multi-object lock retry, and a sharded store to exercise it.
  • Incremental table resize and key-expiry accuracy in mini-redis.
  • A Rust or Go mini-redis for a baseline.
  • Streaming and multipart bodies, offloaded file I/O and exception unwinding in the C.

docs.title: Waiting on a decision
docs.text:

  • Should constants become camelCase too?

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
Step Question Answer in one line 1. Why Strata What does Goose leave out for servers? Dynamic objects, shared state and many lightweight threads. 2. Foundations What do fibers, arenas, refcounts and frames cost? A 4 KB fiber floor, free arena layout choices, no biased counts, about 1 ns per parking call. 3. An HTTP server Can the model carry a real server? Yes: 88 to 94 B per idle connection, throughput syscall-bound. 4. Rust and Go Is it any better than what exists? Memory per connection, yes; pipelined throughput, about 2x; real handlers shrink the gap. 5. mini-redis What does a second, different server break? Cross-worker wakeups, pub/sub backpressure, a shared database. 6. Locks that park How should sync and mutate wait? Park in FIFO order, spin briefly first, acquire several locks all-or-nothing.

All numbers were measured on one machine (Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Linux 6.12, gcc 14.2, rustc 1.93, Go 1.24, OpenJDK 25), usually from single runs. Raw data lives in bench/results/.

docs.title: 1. Why Strata
docs.text:
Goose offers compiler-managed lifetimes, native C output and large virtual-memory reservations that let selected arrays grow in place. Its strict thread isolation and limited dynamic allocation make typical server programs awkward.

Strata keeps those ideas and adds what a server needs:

  • dynamically created objects and graphs with independent lifetimes
  • thousands of virtual threads running ordinary sequential code
  • efficient shared, read-heavy state such as caches
  • deterministic cleanup of files, sockets and locks
  • reference safety without writing lifetime names like 'a

It is not a Goose fork or a Rust dialect, and it does not try for feature parity with Rust. Understandable semantics win over zero overhead at all costs.

docs.title: The first rules
docs.text:
Two rules shaped everything after them, and both came from the user rather than from measurement:

Principle 10: no hidden magic

Aside from virtual threads and parking, nothing happens behind the programmer's back. No implicit buffering, no implicit batching. A library may offer batching, but only when the program asks for it, and it is off by default.

Principle 11: every unbounded input has a limit

A header block, a request body and a parsed document's depth all have limits stated by the program. Big payloads are streamed or spooled to a file, never parsed whole. Exceeding a limit is an error the caller can see.

docs.title: 2. Measuring the foundations
docs.text: Before writing any Strata, the expensive questions got small C benchmarks, compared with Rust (Tokio, slab) and Java virtual threads where one existed. Full tables: group1.md, group2.md, group56.md, lazy.md.

docs.title: Fibers and stacks
docs.text:
Unit (100k idle, 1 KB state) Resident bytes each Tokio task 1,419 (395 with no state) Strata pooled-stack fiber 4,113 (one page floor) Java virtual thread about 809 heap with no state
  • A stackful fiber has a 4 KB floor; a stackless task is about 10x smaller when idle state is small. The gap closes near page size.
  • MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is mandatory with transparent huge pages on: without it a 64 KB stack costs 65 KB resident, and a 1 MB stack almost 1 MB.
  • Per-stack guard pages do not scale: each costs two mappings, and 1M fibers hit the map-count limit.
  • Switching is cheap: about 13 ns with 1k fibers, 35 to 39 ns with 100k.

docs.title: Typed arenas
docs.text:
• Layout (one reservation, a chunk table, or munmap) makes no measurable difference to allocation cost; choose by what handles need.
  • Smaller chunks reclaim better, and geometric growth removes the small-type floor.
  • Against glibc, after freeing everything an arena returns memory (0.3 MB retained against 153 MB).
  • MADV_DONTNEED zero-fills, so a generation stored in a slot is lost when a chunk is decommitted. The fix is a per-chunk epoch kept in the resident chunk header.
  • Long-lived objects scattered through shared chunks pin memory. That is solved by lifetime segregation, which per-type arenas give by construction.

docs.title: Reference counts across threads
docs.text:
• Biased counting is 2 to 7x cheaper than atomic for thread-private objects, but once objects cross threads it is equal or worse (0.71 to 0.87x at 16 threads with message passing).
  • Decision: no biased counting in v1. Types proven thread-confined get plain counts; shared types get plain atomic counts.
  • Messaging stays for passing data, with typed per-vthread mailboxes. Shared memory with sync and mutate is the primary sharing model.

docs.title: Frames for parked calls
docs.text:
Four strategies were compared: plain calls, a heap frame per call (eager), frames embedded in the caller, and lazy frames created only while unwinding a real park.

  • Lazy beats eager by 3.6 ns per request at depth 4 and 7.7 ns at depth 8 when parks are rare. The whole difference between strategies is about 1 ns per parking call.
  • An earlier estimate of 20 to 30 ns saved per request was too high; the measured saving is 4 to 8 ns.
  • Parked memory is the same for lazy and eager.

docs.title: 3. An HTTP server
docs.text: The first proving ground. The server is written as .stra source, with a hand-written C counterpart standing in for compiler output. Tests pin the two together.

docs.title: What it showed
docs.text:
4 workers, 64 active connections per idle connection requests/s Strata-style C, 100k connections 89 B 1.29M Tokio, lazy futures 897 B 1.25M Tokio, naive handler 3,074 B 1.25M
  • The 88 B is sizeof(ConnTask) and nothing else: an idle connection holds no buffer.
  • Throughput is nearly equal because the workload is syscall-bound (about 3 microseconds per request). The frame model buys memory, not a large throughput win.
  • Kernel memory (3 to 3.6 KB per socket) dwarfs all of it and is the same for every server.

docs.title: Features that were added, each from a review
docs.text:
• Size-class input buffers replaced a fixed 2 KB buffer; the reader no longer moves bytes per request.
  • Two body readers: a small in-memory one for APIs (1 MB default) and a file-backed upload reader with a much larger limit. Both refuse an oversize body with 413 before holding it.
  • Pipelined requests run as one child task each, answered in request order, with a barrier for unsafe methods.
  • Opt-in response batching, off by default, with a bound on held responses and a max hold time. It exists to honour principle 10.
  • Lingering close, so an error response is not destroyed by a reset when the client is still sending.
  • Layering: generic support moved into runtime and library files; server.stra holds only the server.

docs.title: Negative controls
docs.text: Each important property has a build that breaks it on purpose (responses in completion order, no body limits, no yield, and so on), and the matching test must fail. 38 tests pass and every control fails as intended.

docs.title: 4. Against Rust and Go
docs.text:
The same design was written in Rust (Tokio) and Go (a pipelined server, and plain net/http), driven by the same tests and load generator.

Pipelined, 1 worker requests/s Strata-style C 4.05M Rust (Tokio) 2.1M Go 2.12M Idle memory per connection bytes Strata-style C 89 to 192 Rust about 1,400 Go 4,000 to 5,000 Go net/http 33,000

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
Caveats

Real handlers do real work, which shrinks the throughput gap a lot. What survives is memory per connection, in-connection concurrency, the timer floor and Go's garbage-collection tail. All runs are single runs on loopback.

Browsers do not pipeline HTTP/1.1 (they multiplex over HTTP/2), so the pipelined number says more about the runtime's cost per request than about web traffic.

docs.title: 5. mini-redis
docs.text:
The second proving ground, chosen because it differs from HTTP: long-lived connections, pub/sub fan-out and one shared database. The server side of tokio-rs/mini-redis was converted (frame, parse, connection, db, server, shutdown, commands).

Conversion depends on no third-party crates

If a program needs a crate, Strata would have no equivalent. The README maps each crate used by the original to a replacement, and lists the standard-library pieces the Strata source assumes.

docs.title: What was new
docs.text:
• Cross-worker wakeups: a publish on one worker must wake a subscriber parked on another.
  • Backpressure: one mailbox per subscriber connection with a declared capacity and an explicit lag policy, Disconnect (default) or Notice.
  • A reaper: cleanup() cannot take a lock, so a dying subscriber hands its subscriptions to a queue, and a purge vthread unsubscribes them.
  • Fairness: a pipelining publisher starved subscribers until each connection yielded every 64 commands.
  • Limits everywhere: frame size, bulk size, key length, key count, topics, subscriptions and queue depth.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Item Result GET/SET 90/10, 1 worker 328k ops/s unpipelined, 468k pipelined 16 deep 4 workers 1.10M to 1.94M; the load generator tops out near 1.3M unpipelined Pub/sub deliveries, 1 / 4 workers 440 to 456k/s / up to 1.98M/s Median delivery latency, 1 worker 12 µs for 1 subscriber, 84 µs for 64, 1.4 ms for 1,000 Idle connection / idle subscriber 297 B / 354 to 594 B

The idle subscriber first cost 4.5 KB because the mailbox ring was allocated at full size; growing it on demand fixed that.

docs.title: Tests and honesty
docs.text:
27 tests pass on six builds (plain, park-only, and both under AddressSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer), with four negative controls. Bugs found along the way included a wake sent to an uninitialised worker and two data races, fixed.

There is no baseline: building the original Rust server was blocked by the permission system, so none of these numbers is compared with Rust.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Entering sync or mutate may park the virtual thread. A holder never parks inside the block (a compile error), so two vthreads on one worker never contend and hold time is bounded by the code in the block.

Several objects in one head, as in mutate(a, b), are acquired all-or-nothing in a fixed global order; if one is busy the acquirer releases everything, parks on that lock's FIFO queue and retries, keeping its arrival ticket. Nested acquisition of another object, reentrancy and read-to-write upgrade are errors.

docs.title: The ordering key
docs.text: The order is by the address of each object's lock word, or (arena id, slot index) for arena objects whose storage can move. A per-allocation sequence number was rejected for its cost. Arenas never compact, and a chunk is freed only when empty, so a live object's address never changes. Only types that appear in a sync or mutate head carry a lock word.

docs.title: The measurement that changed the contract's implementation
docs.text:
With FIFO fairness, one waiting writer makes every later reader queue behind it, and each handoff is a cross-thread wake. Throughput at 4 workers, one lock, 64 connections:

GET share park only spin then park 100% 1.29M 1.29M 90% 570k 1.28M 50% 330k 1.27M 0% 318k 1.27M

A 10% write mix lost 55% of throughput. Spinning 2000 rounds before parking removed the loss. The contract is unchanged (entering still "may park"); only the cost differs. A 100-round spin was noisy, from 1.0M to 326k at 50% reads.

The park-only build remains in the test suite so the handoff path stays covered.

Not yet implemented

The multi-object retry exists only as design. mini-redis has a single lock.
